Working with Arrow and Parquet

Source: vignettes/arrow-parquet.Rmd
arrow-parquet.Rmd

The uint64 problem

A5 cell ids are 64-bit unsigned integers. R has no native uint64 type, and its double can only represent integers exactly up to 2^53. Almost every A5 cell id exceeds this threshold, so converting them to double silently corrupts the data.

This is a problem when reading Parquet files that store A5 cell ids as uint64 columns: the standard format used by DuckDB, Python, and geoparquet.io. By default, arrow::read_parquet() converts uint64 to R’s double, losing precision. The same happens with dplyr::collect() on an Arrow dataset or query.

library(a5R)
#> a5R 1.0.0.9000 • a5 crate 1.0.0 • A5 index 1.0 • 1 thread
library(arrow)
library(tibble)

# A real A5 cell: Edinburgh at resolution 20
cell <- a5_lonlat_to_cell(-3.19, 55.95, resolution = 20)
a5_u64_to_hex(cell)
#> [1] "63bb93f88f080000"

# Write to Parquet as uint64 (the standard interchange format)
tf <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
arrow::write_parquet(
  arrow::arrow_table(cell_id = a5_cell_to_arrow(cell)),
  tf
)

# Read it back naively: arrow silently converts uint64 to double
(naive <- tibble(arrow::read_parquet(tf)))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   cell_id
#>     <dbl>
#> 1 7.19e18

cell_as_dbl <- naive$cell_id

# The double can't distinguish this cell from nearby ids
cell_as_dbl == cell_as_dbl + 1   # TRUE: silent corruption
#> [1] TRUE
cell_as_dbl == cell_as_dbl + 100 # still TRUE
#> [1] TRUE

The solution: a5_cell_from_arrow() and a5_cell_to_arrow()

a5R provides two functions that move ids between a5_cell and Arrow uint64 without passing through double:

# Six cities across the globe. Tokyo and Sydney have bit 63 set: a signed
# int64 would make them negative.
cities <- tibble(
  name = c("Edinburgh", "Tokyo", "São Paulo", "Nairobi", "Anchorage", "Sydney"),
  lon  = c(   -3.19,     139.69,     -46.63,     36.82,    -149.90,    151.21),
  lat  = c(   55.95,      35.69,     -23.55,     -1.29,      61.22,    -33.87)
)

cities$cell <- a5_lonlat_to_cell(cities$lon, cities$lat, resolution = 10)
cities
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   name          lon    lat cell            
#>   <chr>       <dbl>  <dbl> <a5_cell>       
#> 1 Edinburgh   -3.19  56.0  63bb948000000000
#> 2 Tokyo      140.    35.7  872fb48000000000
#> 3 São Paulo  -46.6  -23.6  38a5138000000000
#> 4 Nairobi     36.8   -1.29 6fad7b8000000000
#> 5 Anchorage -150.    61.2  012f4c8000000000
#> 6 Sydney     151.   -33.9  9ca4cf8000000000

Add two ordinary columns to store alongside the cells:

edinburgh <- cities$cell[1]

cities$resolution <- a5_get_resolution(cities$cell)
cities$dist_from_edinburgh_km <- as.numeric(
  a5_cell_distance(cities$cell, rep(edinburgh, nrow(cities)), units = "km")
)

cities
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   name          lon    lat cell             resolution dist_from_edinburgh_km
#>   <chr>       <dbl>  <dbl> <a5_cell>             <int>                  <dbl>
#> 1 Edinburgh   -3.19  56.0  63bb948000000000         10                     0 
#> 2 Tokyo      140.    35.7  872fb48000000000         10                  9233.
#> 3 São Paulo  -46.6  -23.6  38a5138000000000         10                  9743.
#> 4 Nairobi     36.8   -1.29 6fad7b8000000000         10                  7317.
#> 5 Anchorage -150.    61.2  012f4c8000000000         10                  6662.
#> 6 Sydney     151.   -33.9  9ca4cf8000000000         10                 16872.

Writing and reading Parquet

a5_to_arrow_table() converts a data frame to an Arrow table, writing cell columns as native uint64, the binary format DuckDB, Python and geoparquet.io use, and recording the A5 index version in the schema metadata under the key a5_index, which a5px and a5view write too:

tf <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
arrow::write_parquet(a5_to_arrow_table(cities), tf)

a5_from_arrow_table() reads it back, recovering the exact ids. It reads every uint64 column as cells unless cells = names them, and refuses a table tagged with a different index version:

pq <- arrow::read_parquet(tf, as_data_frame = FALSE)
pq$schema
#> Schema
#> name: string
#> lon: double
#> lat: double
#> cell: uint64
#> resolution: int32
#> dist_from_edinburgh_km: double
#> 
#> See $metadata for additional Schema metadata
result <- a5_from_arrow_table(pq)
identical(result$cell, cities$cell)
#> [1] TRUE

For a single column, a5_cell_to_arrow() and a5_cell_from_arrow() convert between a5_cell and an Arrow uint64 array.

Storing coverings

A covering, such as the cells of a polygon, is stored as a list of 64-bit values: its compacted cells in curve order, then a compaction marker recording the resolution they stand for (see vignette("coverings")). This is the layout every A5 library uses, so covering columns are written as list<uint64>, which DuckDB, Python and JavaScript read without losing the resolution:

cities$within_50km <- a5_spherical_cap(cities$cell, radius = 50000)
cities[c("name", "within_50km")]
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   name      within_50km                  
#>   <chr>     <a5_covering>                
#> 1 Edinburgh res 10: 239 cells (62 stored)
#> 2 Tokyo     res 10: 241 cells (64 stored)
#> 3 São Paulo res 10: 244 cells (73 stored)
#> 4 Nairobi   res 10: 238 cells (58 stored)
#> 5 Anchorage res 10: 241 cells (55 stored)
#> 6 Sydney    res 10: 245 cells (74 stored)

tf <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
arrow::write_parquet(a5_to_arrow_table(cities[c("name", "cell", "within_50km")]), tf)
pq <- arrow::read_parquet(tf, as_data_frame = FALSE)
pq$schema
#> Schema
#> name: string
#> cell: uint64
#> within_50km: list<element: uint64>
#> 
#> See $metadata for additional Schema metadata

Reading the table back turns list<uint64> columns into coverings. Coverings written by other A5 libraries are checked, sorted and compacted; an element without a compaction marker stands for the resolution of its finest cell. a5_covering_to_arrow() and a5_covering_from_arrow() convert a single column.

back <- a5_from_arrow_table(pq)
identical(back$within_50km, cities$within_50km)
#> [1] TRUE

Keep the compaction marker when moving coverings through other tools: the stored cells have mixed resolutions, and without the marker nothing records which resolution they stand for. Expand a covering with a5_uncompact() before joining it to data keyed by cell.

Data written by a5R before 1.0

a5R 1.0 uses A5’s permanent cell-ID system. Its space-filling curve threads the cells differently from the index used by a5R 0.6 and earlier (the “v0” index), so every cell has a new id. A v0 id is still a valid cell in the current index, but in a different place, and nothing in the id records which version wrote it. Files written before 1.0 carry no index tag, so a5_from_arrow_table() cannot detect them: convert stored v0 ids exactly once, as they are read.

# A resolution-8 cell id written by a5R 0.6
v0 <- a5_cell("59c4780000000000")
a5_migrate(v0)
#> <a5_cell[1]>
#> [1] 59c4280000000000

a5_migrate() is a bit operation, so it is cheap on large columns. Apply it to every stored id column, including compacted cell sets, which a5R 0.6 stored as plain cell columns (a5_compact(a5_migrate(a5_uncompact(old, resolution = r)))), or re-index the data from its coordinates. Upstream will retire the conversion in a future version.

How it works under the hood

All four converters run in Rust and pass one contiguous uint64 buffer (a list<uint64> for coverings) through the Arrow C data interface, Arrow’s standard in-memory exchange format. The ids never pass through double, and NA cells and missing coverings become nulls. See vignette("internal-cell-representation") for how a5_cell stores ids in R.
